parole.significato: shallow oval tub or tray used for acquiring cream from milk; a type of churn

parole.testo: First attested in the 1830s. Apparently a diminutive in -je or -tje. The first part might be borrowed from West Frisian akkefyt (“chore”), but the further origin is uncertain. The usual explanation connects it with Latin aqua vitae (“liquor, especially spice-flavored”); compare Norwegian akevitt, Ge

parole.significato: one who is extremely poor, a down-and-outer, a beggar
parole.testo: From armoede (“poverty; strife”) + zaaier (“one who sows”), a calque of West Frisian earmoedsaaier (“aggressive, argumentative person”). West Frisian later borrowed the sense “destitute person” from Dutch.
Probably borrowed from West Frisian [Term?] or Dutch Low Saxon [Term?]. Equivalent to deksel + -s as a minced oath for duivels.

parole.significato: sleepy, dozy, not fully awake or to one's senses
parole.testo: Borrowed from West Frisian dûs, ultimately related to Proto-West Germanic *dwās (“stupid”).
Borrowed from West Frisian dolle (“to dig a hole”).
Borrowed from West Frisian fierljeppe, from fier (“far”) + ljeppe (“to leap”).
Borrowed from West Frisian fierljeppen, gerund of the verb fierljeppe.

Variant of vreten (“to eat”), possibly from cognate West Frisian frette or influenced by other cognate forms (compare German fressen, Westphalian Low German friätten, northern Low German frett, third-person singular of freten).

parole.significato: to walk over land while wearing ice skates
to wrangle, to try to get a better price
parole.testo: Possibly from West Frisian pingel (“small item”), or ping(-ping) (“money”); if so, cognate with pinkelen (“pinch”) (English pinch) and pimpel (“small glass”), also "blue tit."

parole.significato: to carry (a heavy object or load), tote, schlep
parole.testo: From West Frisian sjouwe, believed to be from *skiōua, *skiāva (“to slide, shove”), a variant of Old Frisian skūva (“to push, shove”), from Proto-Germanic *skeubaną. Doublet of schuiven, inherited from the same Proto-Germanic root. More at shove.

parole.significato: a long-haired breed of dog originating from Friesland, historically used as retriever, pointer, hound, watchdog and car…
parole.testo: Borrowed from West Frisian stabij. There are some attestations of Staby as a proper noun used of dogs in Dutch texts from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, perhaps as a given name for a dog.

parole.significato: a fortified stone house or tower, a keep
parole.testo: Borrowed from West Frisian stins, shortened from Old Frisian stēnhūs (“stone house”).

parole.significato: artificial mound or hillock used as shelter during high tide
parole.testo: Borrowed from West Frisian terp, from Old Frisian therp, from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, *þrepą (“village, farmstead, troop”), from Proto-Indo-European *treb- (“dwelling, room”). Doublet of dorp.

parole.significato: an old Dutch sailing barge with a round bow, leeboards and a gaff-rigged mast
parole.testo: Borrowed from West Frisian tsjalk. Often considered a diminutive of an unattested Old Frisian cognate of kiel (“keel”).
